articles.title: Pakiabot: The Love That Travels Hand to Hand
articles.dek: Every evening in a Manila jeepney, strangers pass coins down a chain of open palms without a second thought. The apostle John saw the love of God moving the same way.
articles.quote: God's love reaches its finish line only when it passes through your hands to someone else.
articles.illustration: jeepney fare passed hand to hand
articles.body:
It is a quarter past six on Aurora Boulevard, and the rain has turned the jeepney into a small, steamy room on wheels. Fourteen strangers sit knee to knee on two long benches, their shoulders damp and their bags pressed onto their laps. At the very back, near the open door, a college student in a wet uniform digs into her pocket, counts her coins in the dim light, and realizes with a sinking feeling that she is three pesos short. She has nothing else with her, so she leans forward anyway, cheeks warm, and says to the man beside her, "Bayad po, isa lang, estudyante, sa Cubao."

No Filipino ever stops to admire what happens next, because it happens a million times a day. The man takes the coins without looking up from his phone and hands them to the lola beside him. She passes them to a call center agent wearing a lanyard, who passes them to a boy holding a basketball, who reaches over a sleeping construction worker and drops them into the driver's open palm. On this particular evening, though, the call center agent glances at the coins as they cross her hand. Without a word she slips a five-peso coin from her own purse into the little bundle before passing it along. The driver counts by feel, steering with one hand through the flooded street, and sends back two pesos of change down the same chain of strangers. When the student opens her palm and finds the change, she understands at once. She looks up the bench and finds a tired woman in a lanyard smiling at her before turning back to the window, and the jeepney lurches on toward Cubao, carrying fourteen people who for one minute behaved like family.

I have come to believe that the humble pakiabot chain is one of the loveliest pictures of the Christian life our culture has ever given us. It is also remarkably close to what the apostle John was trying to tell a hurting church in the passage we read today.

John was most likely an old man when he wrote this letter, near the end of the first century, to congregations around the city of Ephesus in what is now western Turkey. Those churches had just been through a painful split. Some members had walked out (1 John 2:19), claiming a superior spiritual knowledge while treating their fellow believers with coldness and contempt. The ones who stayed were wounded and unsure. John writes to them as a grandfather would, calling them "dear friends" again and again. The Greek word is agapētoi, which simply means "beloved ones." An ancient tradition, preserved by the church father Jerome, says that when John was too frail to preach, he would be carried into the gathering and would say only, "Little children, love one another." When someone asked why he repeated it so often, he answered that it was the Lord's command, and that if this alone were done, it would be enough.

Read 1 John 4 with that old man in mind and the chapter begins to glow. "Dear friends, let us love one another, for love comes from God," he writes (1 John 4:7). Then he tells them where it started: "This is how God showed his love among us: He sent his one and only Son into the world that we might live through him" (1 John 4:9). He wants them to see clearly that love began with God's move toward us, and so he writes, "This is love: not that we loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son as an atoning sacrifice for our sins" (1 John 4:10). The first coin in the chain was placed by God himself. From there John draws the obvious conclusion: "Dear friends, since God so loved us, we also ought to love one another" (1 John 4:11). And then he writes a sentence that would have made his first readers sit up.

"No one has ever seen God; but if we love one another, God lives in us and his love is made complete in us." (1 John 4:12, NIV)

The opening words would have sounded familiar to anyone who knew John's Gospel, because he had written almost the same line before. In John 1:18 he says, "No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is himself God and is in closest relationship with the Father, has made him known." In the Gospel, the answer to the invisible God is Jesus, walking the roads of Galilee where people could touch him. By the time John writes this letter, Jesus has ascended to the Father, and a fair question hangs in the air: how does anyone see God now? John keeps the same opening and gives it a new ending. The invisible God becomes visible when his people love one another. One way to read this is that the church picks up where the Gospel left off, so that the face of God, once seen in Jesus, is now glimpsed in a woman who quietly covers a student's fare.

The phrase "made complete" deepens the picture. John uses the Greek verb teleioō, built on the word telos, which means a goal, an end point, a finish line. It describes a task brought to its intended conclusion. The same word family appears on Jesus' lips at the cross when he cries, "It is finished" (John 19:30). John is suggesting that God's love has a destination. It arrives in our lives, and it reaches its intended goal when it travels on through us to someone else. A jeepney fare sitting in a passenger's hand has not yet done its job, and it is complete only when it lands in the driver's palm and the change makes its way home.

That is why John can say so plainly, "We love because he first loved us" (1 John 4:19). None of us starts the chain. We are all passengers somewhere in the middle of the bench, receiving what was handed to us and passing it along. Then John adds a sentence that leaves very little room for pretending: "Whoever does not love their fellow believer, whom they have seen, cannot love God, whom they have not seen" (1 John 4:20). The test of our love for the God we cannot see is how we treat the person on the bench beside us, the one we can see, smell, and sometimes find difficult. John even promises that this is a light burden. "His commands are not burdensome," he writes (1 John 5:3), and anyone who has passed a coin down a jeepney knows how little it costs to stretch out a hand.

There is one more gift tucked into this chapter. "There is no fear in love. But perfect love drives out fear" (1 John 4:18). The word translated "perfect" is teleia, from the same root as "made complete." Love that has reached its goal pushes fear out of the room. The student in the back of that jeepney rode in shame for about thirty seconds, and a stranger's five pesos drove it away. Many people around us are sitting with that same quiet fear of being found short, whether of money, of strength, or of worth, and our small acts of love can be the very means God uses to free them.

Before the day ends, think of one person who sits on your bench, perhaps a coworker who is struggling, a sibling you have not spoken to in months, or the guard who opens the door for you every morning. Then pass along one specific kindness, such as a message, a paid merienda, a debt quietly forgiven, or simply your full attention. You do not need to manufacture the love yourself. It was placed in your hand by Someone who loved you first, and passed to you by a mother, a teacher, or a friend who once covered what you lacked. God's love reaches its finish line only when it passes through your hands to someone else. So when it comes to you today, receive it with gratitude, and then lean toward the next person and say, with all the warmth of a Filipino commuter, "Pakiabot po."

articles.title: The Man Who Said “We”
articles.dek: Daniel had one of the cleanest records in Scripture, yet when he prayed for his broken nation, he knelt with the guilty. Heaven's reply tells us how God sees people who pray that way.
articles.quote: Daniel counted himself among the guilty, and heaven answered by calling him treasured.
articles.body:
On a gray December morning in 1970, Willy Brandt, the chancellor of West Germany, walked up to the memorial in Warsaw that honors the Jews who rose up against the Nazis in the ghetto in 1943. He laid a wreath, straightened its ribbon, and stepped back, as every visiting statesman does. Then, with nothing in the official schedule to warn anyone, he sank to his knees on the wet stone and stayed there in silence for about half a minute while the cameras clicked around him.

What made the moment so startling was Brandt's own story. He had fled Germany as a young man in 1933, spent the war years in exile in Norway and Sweden, and worked against Hitler's regime from the outside. If any German leader had a personal right to point at others, it was Brandt. The journalist Hermann Schreiber wrote in Der Spiegel that he knelt as one who had no need to, on behalf of all who needed to and did not. Brandt later explained it simply: under the weight of recent history, he did what people do when words fail them. He received the Nobel Peace Prize the following year, and many historians count that half minute on the stones as a turning point in Germany's long road toward reconciliation with its neighbors.

Twenty-five centuries earlier, another man with clean hands knelt for his people. Daniel 9 opens "in the first year of Darius son of Xerxes" (Daniel 9:1), around 539 BC, just after Babylon fell to the Medes and Persians. Daniel was old by then, probably in his eighties. He had been carried off from Jerusalem as a teenager, had served under several kings, and had already survived a night among lions. One day, reading the scroll of the prophet Jeremiah, he came across the promise that Jerusalem's desolation would last seventy years (Daniel 9:2; Jeremiah 25:11–12; 29:10). He did the arithmetic and realized the time was almost up.

A younger man might have started packing. Daniel prayed instead: "So I turned to the Lord God and pleaded with him in prayer and petition, in fasting, and in sackcloth and ashes" (Daniel 9:3). Sackcloth was the coarse goat-hair cloth of mourners, and ashes on the head were the ancient sign of a heart in grief. What pours out of him is one of the longest prayers of confession in the Bible: "We have sinned and done wrong. We have been wicked and have rebelled; we have turned away from your commands and laws" (Daniel 9:5). The little word we runs through the whole prayer like a thread.

The person saying it makes the prayer remarkable. Daniel's record is one of the cleanest in Scripture. When jealous officials in the Persian court went hunting for something to use against him, "they could find no corruption in him, because he was trustworthy and neither corrupt nor negligent" (Daniel 6:4). His contemporary Ezekiel named him alongside Noah and Job as a model of righteousness (Ezekiel 14:14). He had refused the king's food as a boy and kept praying toward Jerusalem when it was a crime to do so. Yet in this entire prayer he never once says they. He takes the failures of the kings, priests, and ordinary families of Jerusalem and holds them as his own. He even marks the hour of his prayer by "the time of the evening sacrifice" (Daniel 9:21), although no altar had stood in Jerusalem for decades, because his heart still kept the rhythm of a home that lay in ruins.

Then he reaches the center of it all:

"We do not make requests of you because we are righteous, but because of your great mercy. Lord, listen! Lord, forgive! Lord, hear and act! For your sake, my God, do not delay, because your city and your people bear your Name." (Daniel 9:18–19)

Daniel sets his own record aside entirely and rests his case on the character of God. The Hebrew word for mercy here is rachamim, which comes from rechem, the word for womb. It describes the deep, physical tenderness a mother feels for the child she carried. Daniel is appealing to that kind of love, the love that keeps loving a child who has wandered far from home.

The answer came faster than anyone could have expected. While Daniel was still speaking, the angel Gabriel arrived "in swift flight" with this message: "As soon as you began to pray, a word went out, which I have come to tell you, for you are highly esteemed" (Daniel 9:23). The Hebrew behind "highly esteemed" is chamudot, from a root meaning to delight in or desire. Elsewhere in the Old Testament the same family of words describes treasure and precious things. The word comes back twice in the next chapter, when a heavenly messenger addresses him as "Daniel, you who are highly esteemed" and then says, "Do not be afraid, you who are highly esteemed... Peace! Be strong now; be strong" (Daniel 10:11, 19).

One way to read this is that heaven answered the man who said we by calling him treasured. Daniel counted himself among the guilty, and heaven answered by calling him treasured. Standing humbly beside flawed people did nothing to lower him in God's sight, and it seems to have been part of what God delighted in. The posture also points far ahead. Centuries later, Jesus, who had no sin to confess, waded into the Jordan and stood in line with sinners to be baptized (Matthew 3:13–15). Paul would write, "God made him who had no sin to be sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God" (2 Corinthians 5:21). Daniel on his knees in Babylon gives us an early, small picture of the Savior who would kneel beside us.

Most of us find they much easier to say. Filipinos know the reflex well, whether the topic is traffic, corruption in government, the politics in the parish, or the tito whose behavior brought hiya on the whole clan. The family group chat can become a long list of who did what. Daniel shows another way to carry the failures of the people we belong to. He told the truth about what had gone wrong, he included himself in it, and then he trusted the whole matter to the mercy of God. There was no self-hatred in his prayer and no pretending, only an honest heart that chose to stand with its people.

This could look very ordinary in your life. If your family has hurt a neighbor or a relative, you might be the one who finally says, "Pasensya na, we hurt you," even though you personally did nothing wrong. When you pray for the Philippines, you might pray, "Lord, we have tolerated what we should have confronted, and we have been careless with what you gave us." At church or at work, you could be the person who says, "We dropped the ball," and then quietly helps pick it up. Prayers and apologies like these often open doors that years of blaming have kept shut, just as Brandt's silent kneeling did more for peace than a hundred careful speeches.

Tonight, choose one group you belong to (your family, your congregation, your office, or your country) and pray for it in the first person, the way Daniel did. Name its failures gently and honestly, include yourself, and then rest everything on God's great mercy. You may discover what Daniel discovered in Babylon: that a word goes out from heaven the moment you begin to pray, and that the God you approach on your knees already calls you highly esteemed.

articles.title: What the King Kept Closest
articles.dek: Among Tutankhamun's gold, archaeologists found a tiny coffin that held a lock of a grandmother's hair. Psalm 135 uses a Hebrew word for exactly that kind of treasure, and it uses it for God's people.
articles.quote: The God who keeps the winds in his storehouses keeps his people somewhere closer, among the few things he holds in his own hand.
articles.illustration: Queen Tiye's hair in Tutankhamun's tomb
articles.body:
In November 1922, in the Valley of the Kings in Egypt, Howard Carter made a small opening in a sealed doorway, held up a candle, and looked into the tomb of Tutankhamun. His patron, Lord Carnarvon, stood behind him and asked whether he could see anything. Carter is remembered as answering, "Yes, wonderful things." Over the next ten years he and his team cleared and catalogued more than five thousand objects: gilded shrines, chariots, jewelled collars, thrones, and the famous gold mask that has since become the face of ancient Egypt for the whole world.

One of the smallest finds is the one I keep coming back to. In the room Carter called the Treasury, inside a modest wooden box, lay a set of miniature coffins nested one inside another, the innermost no longer than a man's hand. It was inscribed with the name of Queen Tiye, the great royal wife of Amenhotep III, whom most scholars believe to have been Tutankhamun's grandmother. Inside, wrapped in linen, was a carefully braided lock of brown hair. In 2010, DNA testing linked that hair to a mummy long known only as the "Elder Lady," and her identity as Tiye was confirmed.

The boy king died at about nineteen, surrounded by more gold than most of us could picture. Yet among everything sent with him into the dark was a keepsake of a woman from his own family, folded small and kept safe. Filipinos understand this instinct well. We keep a child's first curl in an envelope at the back of the aparador, a folded photo behind the cards in a wallet, a rosary from a parent who has passed on. Every family has its official possessions, and then it has the few things it keeps close because they are loved.

Psalm 135 has a word for that second kind of treasure, and it uses it in a surprising place. This is a hallelujah psalm, one of the hymns Israel sang at the temple, probably in the years after the exile when a smaller, humbled people had returned to Jerusalem and rebuilt their worship. Its first word is hallelu Yah, literally "praise the LORD," and it borrows freely from older scriptures, the way a congregation stitches together the songs it already knows by heart. Psalm 134, just before it, ends with servants of the Lord lifting their hands in the sanctuary at night, and Psalm 135 picks up the same company and calls them forward.

Imagine the scene the opening verses paint. The priests and Levites are standing in the courts of the temple, the stone still warm from the day, the crowd of worshippers pressing in behind them. The psalmist calls out to them three times in quick succession: "Praise the LORD. Praise the name of the LORD; praise him, you servants of the LORD, you who minister in the house of the LORD, in the courts of the house of our God" (Psalm 135:1–2). Then he gives the first reason: "Praise the LORD, for the LORD is good; sing praise to his name, for that is pleasant" (Psalm 135:3). And then he gives the reason that seems to have moved him most.

"For the LORD has chosen Jacob to be his own, Israel to be his treasured possession." (Psalm 135:4)

The Hebrew word behind "treasured possession" is segullah. It shows up only a handful of times in the Old Testament, and its meaning becomes vivid when you see where else it appears. When King David gathered materials for the temple, he first gave from the royal stores, and then he added something more personal. "Besides," he said, "in my devotion to the temple of my God I now give my personal treasures of gold and silver" (1 Chronicles 29:3). "Personal treasures" there is segullah. It meant a king's private holdings, set apart from the wealth of the state, the things that belonged to him as a person. Scholars have found a related word in ancient texts from Ugarit, on the Syrian coast, where a great king could call a favored ruler under his care his own segullah, his special possession.

What moves me is where the psalmist sets this word. Read a few lines further and the camera pulls back to the whole sky. "I know that the LORD is great, that our Lord is greater than all gods. The LORD does whatever pleases him, in the heavens and on the earth, in the seas and all their depths. He makes clouds rise from the ends of the earth; he sends lightning with the rain and brings out the wind from his storehouses" (Psalm 135:5–7). The word for "storehouses" is otsarot, the ordinary word for a treasury or a warehouse. So within four verses the psalm names two kinds of treasure belonging to God. One is the vast public treasury of creation, with its clouds and lightning and winds kept in reserve. The other is his segullah, the small, close, personal treasure, and the psalm says that one is a people.

God said the same thing at Sinai, with the same order of thought: "out of all nations you will be my treasured possession. Although the whole earth is mine" (Exodus 19:5). The God who owns every storm chose to keep something near his heart, and what he chose was human beings. One way to read Psalm 135 is that the psalmist praises God's greatness in verses 5 to 7 precisely because of verse 4. A small God with a favorite people would be easy to imagine. A God great enough to command the wind, who still keeps people close the way a king keeps a lock of his grandmother's hair, is worth a temple full of singing.

The name in verse 4 is worth a second look too. The psalm says God chose "Jacob," the old name of the patriarch who grabbed his brother's heel at birth and spent half his life scheming. Moses explained long before that the choosing had nothing to do with Israel's size or quality: "The LORD did not set his affection on you and choose you because you were more numerous than other peoples, for you were the fewest of all peoples. But it was because the LORD loved you" (Deuteronomy 7:7–8). The treasure is precious because of the one who holds it. The New Testament opens this same word to everyone who belongs to Christ, who "gave himself for us to redeem us from all wickedness and to purify for himself a people that are his very own" (Titus 2:14), and Peter calls the church "God's special possession" (1 Peter 2:9).

This is a gentle word for a Monday at the end of November. The Christmas rush has begun, the bills are lining up, and many of us spend our days feeling like one more line item in someone else's inventory, an employee number, a queue ticket, a name on a long list. Psalm 135 lets you see yourself from heaven's side. You belong to the God who measures out the wind, and in his house you are kept in the small box near his heart, among the few things he would never trade.

The psalmist's own response was praise, and he called it "pleasant" (Psalm 135:3), the kind of singing that comes easily when you finally believe you are loved. You might copy verse 4 onto a small card today, writing your own name in place of "Jacob," and tuck it into your wallet beside the photos you already carry. When the day makes you feel small, take it out and read what God says about the people he keeps.

Howard Carter needed ten years and thousands of entries to record what lay in that tomb, and most visitors today walk straight past the tiny coffin to look at the gold. God's catalogue works the other way around. The God who keeps the winds in his storehouses keeps his people somewhere closer, among the few things he holds in his own hand. Whatever this week asks of you, you can walk into it as someone who has already been chosen, kept, and treasured.

articles.title: The Gift of a Faithful Wound
articles.dek: A missionary surgeon in India found that pain was protecting his patients. Solomon had found the same thing about friendship nearly three thousand years earlier.
articles.quote: A friend's honest words hurt for the same reason pain does: something is wrong, and someone cares enough to warn you.
articles.illustration: Paul Brand and the gift of pain
articles.body:
In the late 1940s, a young British surgeon named Paul Brand began working with leprosy patients at the Christian Medical College in Vellore, in southern India. Brand had been born in India to missionary parents, and he brought their compassion with him into the operating room. What he saw there troubled him deeply. His patients were missing fingers, toes, and sometimes whole sections of their feet, and nearly everyone at the time assumed that the disease itself was slowly eating away their flesh.

Brand watched more closely and came to a different conclusion. Leprosy, he found, mainly attacks the nerves. Once those nerves die, the hands and feet stop sending warnings, and the damage comes afterward, from ordinary life. A man would grip a hot cooking pot and feel nothing. A woman would walk all day on a stone lodged in her sandal and never limp. Some patients were even bitten by rats while they slept, because nothing in their bodies told them to wake up. The tissue itself was healthy enough; what it had lost was the alarm.

This is one of the quiet wonders of the human body. Your skin is full of specialized nerve endings called nociceptors, whose whole job is to report harm, and they never fully rest. Even while you sleep they make you uncomfortable enough to shift position, so that blood keeps reaching every part of your skin. People born with a rare condition that leaves them unable to feel pain often suffer broken bones that go unnoticed and find wounds only when they see the blood. Brand spent the rest of his life telling anyone who would listen that pain is one of God's kindest gifts, and decades later he wrote a book with Philip Yancey whose title said it plainly: The Gift of Pain.

Solomon, writing about friendship long before Brand, arrived at the same truth. The proverbs in this part of the book belong to a collection described in Proverbs 25:1 as "more proverbs of Solomon, compiled by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah." These were Solomon's sayings, gathered by royal scribes generations later because they were too valuable to lose. Chapter 27 opens with warnings about the mouth: do not boast about tomorrow (27:1), and let someone else do your praising (27:2). It moves on to the crushing weight of a fool's provocation and the overwhelming force of jealousy (27:3–4). Then, as if answering the question of what a person truly needs from the people around them, Solomon writes two lines about honesty.

"Better is open rebuke than hidden love," he says in Proverbs 27:5. Love that stays silent while a friend walks toward the edge, simply to keep the peace, does that friend no good at all. Then comes the verse that sits at the heart of the passage:

"Wounds from a friend can be trusted, but an enemy multiplies kisses." (Proverbs 27:6)

The phrase translated "can be trusted" comes from the Hebrew root aman, the same root that gives us the word "amen." It describes something firm and reliable, something you can safely lean your full weight on. Solomon is saying that the sting from a true friend is the kind of thing you can say amen to, because it holds and you can build a life on it. The wound is faithful because the one who gave it is faithful.

The second half of the verse is just as striking. The Hebrew word behind "multiplies" is rare, and scholars have long weighed its meaning; the King James Version renders it "deceitful," while others suggest "profuse" or "excessive." Either way, the picture is of affection poured on too thickly, kisses that keep coming because they cost the giver nothing. In the ancient Near East a kiss was a common greeting between friends and relatives, which is exactly what made a false one so dangerous. Every reader of the Gospels remembers the garden at night and Jesus asking, "Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?" (Luke 22:48).

Paul Brand's discovery opens up this proverb in a fresh way. A friend's honest words hurt for the same reason pain does: something is wrong, and someone cares enough to warn you. The sting might point to a habit that is wearing you down, a temper that is costing you your children's trust, a spending pattern that will eventually catch up with you, or a relationship that is pulling you away from God. The flatterer works like numbness in the body. Their constant reassurance feels pleasant, and meanwhile the damage keeps happening, unfelt, until one day you look down and wonder how you lost so much.

Filipinos understand both sides of this from experience. We treasure pakikisama, the grace of getting along, and we feel hiya keenly, so few of us want to be the one who embarrasses a friend or spoils the mood at a family gathering. We smile, we say "okay lang," and we let things pass. Most of us also know the hurt of discovering that someone we trusted was "plastic," sweet to our face and different behind our back. Proverbs 27:6 gives us a better path than either silence or flattery. A true friend loves you enough to risk the awkward moment, and a wise person learns to treasure the friend who does.

The deepest comfort in this passage comes from the Friend who was wounded for us. Jesus told his disciples, "Greater love has no one than this: to lay down one's life for one's friends" (John 15:13), and in the same breath he called them his friends. He was also the most honest friend they ever had. He told Peter to his face that he would deny him three times before the rooster crowed (Luke 22:34), and after the resurrection he restored him beside a charcoal fire on the shore. To the church in Laodicea, which believed it was rich and needed nothing, the risen Christ said, "Those whom I love I rebuke and discipline" (Revelation 3:19). Every correction from him comes from a Friend who fully intends to heal.

He went further than any human friend ever could. Isaiah, looking ahead to the Messiah, wrote that "he was pierced for our transgressions" and that "by his wounds we are healed" (Isaiah 53:5). The truest wounds in all of Scripture were the ones Jesus received in our place. Because of the cross, a believer can hear hard truth without falling apart, since our standing before God was settled by his wounds and does not depend on our being right about everything. A person secure in grace can afford to be corrected, and the gospel frees us from the exhausting work of defending our pride.

That security changes how we receive a friend's honesty. When someone we trust says something that stings, our first instinct is usually to explain ourselves, to defend, or to quietly avoid that person for a while. A wiser response is to thank them, bring their words to God in prayer, and ask honestly whether the pain is pointing to something real. The psalmist actually prayed for this kind of friend: "Let a righteous man strike me, that is a kindness; let him rebuke me, that is oil on my head" (Psalm 141:5).

It also changes how we offer honesty to others. Solomon speaks of wounds from a friend, which suggests that the right to say hard things is usually earned through years of faithful presence. Jesus taught that when a brother or sister sins, we should "go and point out their fault, just between the two of you" (Matthew 18:15), privately and before anyone else hears of it. A faithful wound is given in person, with love that is easy to see and with healing in view, the way a good surgeon cuts only in order to restore.

Perhaps today you could name one person who has earned the right to tell you the truth, and over coffee or a quiet merienda ask them, "Is there anything you see in me that I might be missing?" Listen without defending yourself, and thank them warmly, even if the answer stings a little. Paul Brand spent his life showing that the sensation we work hardest to avoid is often the very thing that keeps us whole. A friend who loves you enough to hurt you a little is one of God's clearest gifts, and Jesus, who was wounded for you, is the Friend you can trust with every hard word he speaks.
